Overview: Kaspersky presents findings from its 2026 Security Services Global Report, highlighting MDR statistics and the gap between potential and actual breach detection.

Key Topics: More than two high-severity incidents detected daily via Kaspersky MDR; IT and government sectors leading in human-driven attacks; suspicious activity visible weeks before action; and compromise assessment as proactive threat hunting.

Technical Details: Two-thirds of incidents show suspicious activity hidden in endpoints and network traffic for weeks. Nearly 20% of 2025 incidents were discovered manually after bypassing automated controls, exposing blind spots in log-centric SOCs.

Takeaways: Automated controls alone miss sophisticated threats. Organizations need proactive compromise assessments and MDR to detect footholds before breaches materialize.

Security Services Structure

Alexander Zaytsev leads Kaspersky's Security Services Expertise Center, organizing work into offensive, defensive, and threat-intelligence streams. Together they provide a holistic view of customer security posture from both attacker and defender perspectives.

Lifecycle Service Portfolio

Services map to attack stages: Digital Footprint Intelligence and Brand Protection for reconnaissance, Security Assessment and penetration testing for simulated attacks, Compromise Assessment for hunting latent intrusions, Incident Response for containment, MDR for continuous monitoring, and SOC Consulting for operational maturity.

Offensive-Defensive Feedback Loop

Combining offensive and defensive expertise in one center creates a self-reinforcing system. Pentesters learn how SOC teams detect attacks, while defenders incorporate real attacker tradecraft from assessment findings.

Emerging Threat Trends

Zaytsev highlights trusted-relationship and supply-chain attacks where adversaries compromise low-security partners to reach larger targets via VPNs or stolen credentials. He also warns of increasingly destructive attacks where detection-to-impact windows can be minutes, demanding faster response processes.

talks.title: Evgeny Goncharov on protecting the systems that run our world
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for ICS CERT Expertise Center: Evgeny Goncharov on protecting the systems that run our world.
talks.summary:
OT Cybersecurity Scope

Kaspersky ICS CERT head Evgeny Goncharov defines operational technology security as protecting plants, transport, and smart infrastructure from attacks that stop production or cause physical harm—not just data theft.

Common Incident Patterns

Ransomware on IT systems often halts manufacturing because OT, logistics, and business networks are tightly coupled. A U.S. auto-dealer software supplier encryption incident cost clients over a billion dollars in three weeks.

Supply Chain and Regulations

Niche vendors with weak security become industry bottlenecks. Goncharov argues cybersecurity must be designed into cars, nuclear plants, and buildings early because retrofitting is impractical without strong regulation.

People and Emerging Tech

Industrial security blends IT security and engineering cultures. Kaspersky's ML anomaly detection on plant telemetry already flags attacks and operator mistakes, while IIoT and edge computing outpace current security tooling.

talks.title: Dmitry Shmoylov on building security from the ground up
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Threat Research Expertise Center: Dmitry Shmoylov on building security from the ground up.
talks.summary:
Role

Dmitry Shmoylov heads software security at Kaspersky, driving secure development lifecycle (SDLC/SSDLC) across products whose failures would be especially consequential given elevated privileges.

Investment and culture

Secure development can consume 15–20% of team capacity early and slows delivery, requiring involvement from developers through executives, security champions, standardized security gates, extensive tooling, and an active bug bounty program.

Challenges

High-privilege security products attract attackers; continuous control is essential. Checkbox security is insufficient—consistency release-to-release matters organization-wide.

Secure by design and cyberimmunity

Security must be architectural, not patchwork; KasperskyOS embeds controls at the OS level. Cyberimmunity balances security goals with business constraints so protections focus where exploitation cost to attackers is meaningful.

Lessons

Recent pentests and static-analysis gaps on optimized system code and widely used open-source libraries led to CVE filings and improved detection rules.

talks.title: Vladimir Kuskov on the threats that hide in plain sight
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Threat Research Expertise Center: Vladimir Kuskov on the threats that hide in plain sight.
talks.summary:
## SparkCat: App Store Stealer

Kaspersky Anti-Malware Research head Vladimir Kuskov discusses SparkCat, the first large-scale iOS stealer distributed through official app stores. Discovery began when Android Play Market monitoring flagged dynamically loaded code; cross-platform investigation found Rust-based apps using machine vision to scan photo galleries for cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases.

## Evasion and Moderation Gaps

Apps posed as legitimate delivery and editing tools with real functionality plus hidden payloads. Heavy obfuscation and iOS research barriers made analysis difficult. Apple and Google removed apps after disclosure—rare for iOS, where malicious titles seldom reach consumers.

## Firmware and EDR Bypass Trends

Kuskov outlines UEFI threat scanning developed as bootkit samples proliferated, plus defenses against vulnerable-driver abuse that collapses kernel-user isolation. Attackers increasingly block EDR telemetry via firewall rules—legitimate OS capabilities repurposed—requiring vendors to harden self-protection across Windows versions.

## Threat Intelligence as Product

Kaspersky's ATT&CK-aligned intelligence portal lets customers filter by region, industry, and platform to prioritize detection rules. Unlike generic framework examples, Kaspersky supplies command-line samples, file hashes, and ready-made YARA-style guidance—aiming to replace manual parsing of thousands of annual threat reports for SOC tier-three analysts.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Explaining blockchain, cryptocurrency and NFT in a one-dollar bill example.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this discussion, Ivan Imhoff breaks down the fundamental concepts behind blockchain, cryptocurrency, and non-fungible tokens (NFTs) using relatable analogies such as a one-dollar bill. The conversation explores the roots of Web3, contrasting traditional trust-based systems with decentralized, trustless environments, and reviews market volatility cycles as well as emerging utilitarian use cases for digital tokens.

### Key Topics
- **Understanding Blockchain:** Described as a sequential digital accounting ledger where validated transactions link back to all preceding transactions, creating an immutable, irreversible, and uneraseable record.
- **Trustless Systems vs. Traditional Trust:** Traditional finance, tech platforms, and art ownership require trusting intermediaries like banks, governments, Google, or Facebook. In contrast, blockchain operates in a trustless environment where verification occurs automatically without relying on third parties.
- **Fungibility and NFTs:** Standard currency and crypto tokens are fungible (like exchanging standard one-dollar bills). In contrast, an NFT is a non-fungible token representing a unique identifier on the blockchain, comparable to drawing a unique design onto a specific dollar bill so it can no longer be interchanged.
- **The Evolution of NFTs:** While initial adoption centered on hype, scarcity, art, and collectibles (such as CryptoPunks and Bored Ape Yacht Club), the sector is moving toward utilitarian value. Practical applications include event ticketing/registration, community access, and automated royalty distributions directly programmed for creators like musicians.
- **Market Cycles and Volatility:** Historical crypto market patterns feature dramatic bull and bear cycles roughly every three to four years, often pegged to Bitcoin halving phases and driven by human emotion and hype.

### Technical Details
- **Ledger Structure:** Each piece of the blockchain represents a batch of transactions validated at once, chained sequentially to all previous transactions back to origin.
- **Immutability:** Once transactions are validated on the ledger, they cannot be erased, altered, or reversed.
- **Programmed Royalties:** NFTs allow logic to be embedded directly into tokens, enabling automated revenue distribution (e.g., compensating an artist each time a song is played) without central entities like record labels.
- **Asset Classification:** Cryptocurrencies and NFTs behave as risk-on tech assets subject to extreme volatility, with drawdowns of 95% or more following major bull runs.

### Takeaways
- **Value in Bear Markets:** Correction periods—which may last from six months to two years—provide the best opportunity to build, learn, code, and identify enduring projects after speculative excess is flushed out.
- **Utility Over Hype:** Long-term sustainability for NFTs relies on shifting from pure collectibles and speculative art to real-world utility such as access, licensing, and automated revenue sharing.
- **Market Psychology:** Understanding recurring multi-year cycle dynamics helps navigate fear, euphoria, and extreme volatility without succumbing to emotional decision-making.

talks.title: How Fakecalls pretends to be a bank employee
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning How Fakecalls pretends to be a bank employee.
talks.summary:
Fakecalls is a sophisticated Korean Trojan malware targeting customers of Korean banks, specifically mimicking apps from Kookmin Bank and KakaoBank. The malware displays authentic bank support phone numbers harvested from official websites to appear legitimate.

The attack mechanism is elegant: when a user calls their bank's official hotline, Fakecalls detects the outgoing call, silently terminates the connection, and displays a fake call screen. The victim, unaware of the interception, is then routed to attackers posing as bank employees. The Trojan requests extensive permissions including access to contacts, microphone, camera, geolocation, and call control—typical for banking trojans but particularly dangerous in this context.

After intercepting a call, Fakecalls operates in two possible modes. It can directly connect the victim to human scammers disguised as bank support staff, or it can take control of the conversation itself using AI-generated voice responses. Currently, the voice imitation is limited to standard phrases in Korean typical of answering machines and call-center employees. The attackers exploit the false trust created by the victim initiating the contact, using social engineering to extract sensitive information such as payment data, login credentials, CVV codes, and verification codes.

A key vulnerability is the language mismatch: if the phone's interface is in English but suddenly displays a Korean call screen, users may detect the deception. However, for Korean-language users, this red flag disappears.

Kaspersky detects the threat as 'Trojan-Banker.AndroidOS.Fakecalls.' Recommended defenses include: download apps only from official app stores where security scanning occurs; carefully review and deny unnecessary permissions, especially for calls and messages; never disclose personal or financial information over the phone; verify suspicious calls by hanging up and contacting the bank directly via their official website; and install reputable cybersecurity solutions.

## Overview

This interview features Ivan Kwiatkowski, a senior security researcher at Kaspersky's GReAT team, discussing his specialization in reverse engineering and his journey in cybersecurity. The interviewer, Liza, explores how he entered the field, what aspects he finds most engaging, and offers insights for aspiring security professionals.

## How He Entered Cybersecurity

Ivan began his cybersecurity career at age 19 while studying general computer science. He developed an interest in Wi-Fi security, took online classes, and never left the field. He emphasizes that his early introduction and consistent engagement set the foundation for his career.

## Reverse Engineering Focus

Although he initially thought offensive penetration testing would be his preferred specialization, Ivan discovered his passion for reverse engineering—reading and understanding malware code. He explains his preference by noting that unlike penetration testing, where success is uncertain, reverse engineering through persistent effort always yields results. This certainty of eventual success through hard work is what he values most.

## Challenges and Rewards

The most challenging aspect of the job is maintaining persistence. Hours spent analyzing seemingly meaningless instructions and CPU operations can be mentally draining and feels "against nature." However, the satisfaction comes from eventual success after sustained effort—a feeling that drives him forward despite the difficulty.

## Notable Discovery

Ivan's proudest achievement was connecting new traces of malicious activity called "Tomiris" to the existing SolarWinds incident. This discovery was significant because it identified previously unnoticed connections to a major case that impacted the world.

## Career Advice

He recommends newcomers only pursue cybersecurity if they are genuinely passionate, as the learning curve is steep and requires substantial personal commitment. Success requires doing what you love and persisting until you achieve your goals.

## Learning Preferences and Tools

Regarding learning methods, Ivan has evolved from using videos to preferring books and articles for their efficiency in accessing specific knowledge. Regarding tools, he mentions that while he long relied on Iproat, recent developments in Ghidra (an open-source alternative) suggest a viable transition path.

## Culture and Practical Insights

On naming malware or APT groups, he prefers clever or funny names over formal conventions. For media recommendations, he cites Mr. Robot (seasons 1–5) as uniquely accurate in technical representation. He also highlights an effective but seemingly counterintuitive protective measure: regularly rebooting phones can remove sophisticated malware that does not persist across reboots.

talks.summary:
## Overview
Christina Shingareva, Head of External Relations at Kaspersky, discusses how businesses can build effective alliances and cooperate with nonprofit organizations to tackle cybersecurity threats at scale. She explains that while cybersecurity threats have become mainstream public knowledge, the amplified visibility stems from organizations uniting to research and solve issues collaboratively.

## Key Topics

### No More Ransom Project
Launched in 2016 by Europol, the Netherlands Police, Kaspersky, and McAfee, this initiative helps ransomware victims recover encrypted data for free without paying criminals. Kaspersky experts locate decryption keys for various ransomware families and share them. The project now has over 160 global partners and represents a collaborative approach to a problem without a universal single-day solution.

### Coalition Against Stalkerware
Created at the end of 2019, this coalition addresses "surveillance phone" applications sold legally as parental controls but used for tracking and abuse. Currently includes over 40 partner organizations—cybersecurity companies, academia, domestic violence service organizations, law enforcement, and Interpol as a supporter. The coalition recognized stalkerware as both a technical and social issue requiring diverse expertise.

### Tinycheck Tool
An open-source, free scanning tool developed by Kaspersky in response to a French NGO's request. It runs on Raspberry Pi or Linux devices to detect stalkerware by scanning outgoing traffic without alerting the abuser—critical since stalkerware can notify abusers of detection attempts, potentially escalating domestic violence. The tool is designed for use only by NGOs with trained representatives alongside victims to develop safety and escape plans.

## Technical Details
Stalkerware detection presents a regulatory challenge: Kaspersky can detect stalkerware but cannot flag it as malicious or block it due to its legal status. The response was deploying privacy alerts in products that explicitly explain surveillance capabilities (location tracking, text/call interception, activity monitoring) to users.

## Takeaways
- Successful coalitions address real external needs rather than artificial problems
- Partnerships work best when partners possess fundamentally different expertise
- Social issue projects require significant time and resources; the No More Ransom project continues after five years; Coalition Against Stalkerware remains in early stages after two years
- Direct business profit is unlikely; internal organizational buy-in requires substantial PR and reputation investment to justify initiatives without immediate financial returns

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this session presented in partnership with Kaspersky, yoga teacher and personal trainer Shona Vertue leads a 15-minute physical routine tailored specifically for individuals suffering from "tech neck"—strain caused by hovering over digital devices throughout the day. Framing the session around the idea that updating software or phones can feel like a nuisance, Vertue notes that physical posture also requires regular resets and patches to keep moving smoothly and prevent physical decline.

### Key Topics
- Counteracting Tech Neck: Addressing the physical strain, neck stiffness, and poor spinal alignment resulting from long hours spent bent over screens and handheld devices.
- Controlled Articular Rotations (CARs): Isolating joint movements to evaluate, maintain, and expand true active mobility without compensatory shifting from the torso or hips.
- Postural Strength and Spinal Health: Moving through spinal extension, flexion, and lateral stretches to relieve compression and reset posture.
- Glute and Core Activation: Engaging stabilizing muscles such as the glutes and core to protect the lower back and support optimal movement patterns.

### Technical Details
- Neck Controlled Articular Rotations & Range Checks: Participants brace the spine, arm, and chest muscles by making fists, then guide the chin down, laterally toward the collarbone, and into slow, controlled circles. This isolates neck mobility from chest or hip compensation. This is followed by head turns to observe lateral discrepancies, reinforcing that mobility operates on a "use it or lose it" principle.
- Forearm, Chest, and Lateral Stretches: Interlaced finger extensions over the head stretch the forearms and fingers. Combining hand-behind-head thoracic extension with forward flexion synchronizes movement with breathing, followed by seated side bends keeping the opposite hip anchored to elongate the spine.
- Cat-Cow and Contralateral Stability: On all fours, participants mobilize the spine vertebra by vertebra. Contralateral extensions (bird-dog variations) require extending one leg back while keeping a neutral lumbar spine (avoiding an arched "banana back") via core bracing and glute contraction, pairing arm extensions and bringing knee to elbow.
- Pigeon Pose Variation: Transitioning from all fours by extending one leg back and externally rotating the front leg, participants sink hips back toward the floor. To build active hip and leg strength rather than purely passive stretching, participants perform pulses where fingertips lift off the floor.
- Active Cobra and Floor Cooldown: Lying prone, active cobra repetitions emphasize chin retraction, shoulder blade retraction, glute contraction, and engagement of back extensors. The routine concludes with wide-knee child's pose, supine knee-to-chest rocking, Pavanamuktasana (wind-removing pose) to massage the ascending colon, gentle spinal twists, and a brief resting breathwork sequence.

### Takeaways
- Routine physical breaks are vital to protect posture and mobility when working long hours around digital technology.
- True mobility requires isolated joint control; compensating with other body parts masks mobility deficits.
- Combining active glute engagement and core stability safeguards the lumbar spine during movement.
- Taking a short break for physical recovery pairs naturally with taking time to let devices run necessary resets and updates.

talks.summary:
### Overview
This discussion explores the practical application and necessity of threat intelligence and cyber attribution for organizations navigating today's threat landscape. The speakers examine whether pinpointing specific adversaries matters to enterprise defense, how organizations can contextualize threat intelligence to fit their business requirements, and how the economic and technological landscape of security operations is shifting.

### Key Topics
- **The Value of Attribution**: The speakers debate whether attributing an attack to a nation-state, cyber criminal gang, or hacktivist makes an operational difference. Attribution is predominantly critical when there are legal or law enforcement implications that require presenting evidence in a court of law. For general defense, attributing mass-scale, sprayed attacks (such as mass scanning or credential brute forcing) is largely impractical, whereas understanding exposure to specific attack patterns—such as MageCart-style tactics—offers direct defensive value.
- **Contextualization and Asset Mapping**: Threat intelligence is defined as a combination of technology and people that must be shaped around an organization's specific threat landscape. Merely ingesting data feeds without correlating them to an internal asset database leads to spiraling costs without actionable cyber risk reduction.
- **Sourcing Diverse Intelligence**: Organizations are advised not to rely on a single vendor or supplier. A resilient threat intelligence capability incorporates open-source intelligence, US-based vendors, Chinese vendors, and built-in intelligence from next-generation SIEM engines and SOC platforms to gain a truly global perspective.
- **Economics and Operational Shifts**: The cost of monitoring and Security Operations Center (SOC) capabilities is decreasing significantly due to automation and modern toolsets. Capabilities that previously cost £50 to £60 per user per month in large multinationals can now be acquired for around £10 per user per month.

### Technical Details
- **Attacks & Threat Vectors**: Covers broad, automated campaigns including mass port/vulnerability scanning, mass credential brute forcing, and web skimming/targeting exemplified by MageCart actors.
- **Infrastructure & Monitoring**: Ingestion of data feeds into next-generation SIEM platforms and SOC architectures, tied directly to an organization's internal asset inventory to prevent data overload and uncontrolled expense.

### Takeaways
- Focus threat intelligence on protecting critical internal assets and understanding relevant adversary TTPs (like MageCart) rather than obsessing over naming individual threat actors, unless preparing cases for law enforcement.
- Contextualize feeds against your business environment and asset databases to control costs and deliver measurable risk reduction.
- Take advantage of descending SOC and monitoring costs brought by next-generation automated tooling, and engage in open public discussions to train the next generation of security professionals.

talks.summary:
### Overview
This walkthrough demonstrates how to set up and configure a corporate workspace within the Kaspersky Security Center Cloud Console to prepare for deploying security solutions across company devices. The process assumes the administrator already holds a single account for Kaspersky products.

### Key Topics
- Connecting to the Kaspersky Security Center Cloud Console and accepting necessary legal agreements.
- Configuring company details, workspace parameters, and selecting appropriate data centers.
- Choosing between commercial activation codes and 30-day trial workspaces.
- Completing the initial setup using the automated Quick Start Wizard.
- Configuring network settings, Kaspersky Security Network (KSN) participation, and deploying Network Agent packages.

### Technical Details
- **Workspace Creation**: Administrators access the cloud console via a web browser under an existing Kaspersky account, accept the agreements and privacy policy, and enter the company and workspace names. The country selected directly determines the data center where operational data is processed (with mappings documented in the online help). Workspace sizing accommodates device counts ranging from 300 to 10,000.
- **Licensing Considerations**: Users can supply a commercial activation code or request a trial workspace. A trial workspace lasts for 30 days only, has specific documented limitations, and the current version does not support migrating settings from a trial workspace to a commercial one.
- **Provisioning Wait Time**: Creation takes time; users must wait for a confirmation email containing the access link rather than clicking immediately on the webpage.
- **Quick Start Wizard**: Launches automatically upon first connection to create necessary policies, tasks, and software installation packages.
- **Agent & Solution Selection**: Requires deploying Kaspersky Network Agent and security applications on target computers. Kaspersky Network Agent for Windows and Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Windows are selected by default. Proxy server parameters can be supplied if endpoints route traffic through a proxy.
- **Kaspersky Security Network (KSN)**: Provides real-time threat intelligence to increase detection rates for emerging threats. Disabling KSN is noted to significantly weaken endpoint protection.
- **Standalone Installation Package**: The wizard generates a unique standalone installation package for the Network Agent. This package is an executable file digitally signed with a Kaspersky certificate, containing the distribution files preconfigured with specific connection parameters for that distinct workspace.

### Takeaways
- Proper initial planning regarding company location is vital because it locks in data center placement.
- Because trial workspace settings cannot be migrated to commercial workspaces in this version, organizations should evaluate whether a trial or immediate commercial deployment is appropriate.
- The Quick Start Wizard automates the core baseline—generating workspace-specific, signed Network Agent packages, default tasks, and policies—to streamline endpoint onboarding.

## Overview
This Black Hat 2020 preview talk discusses significant cybersecurity campaigns and threat actor activities observed in 2019 and early 2020, focusing on targeted exploitation of activists and evolving Russian threat actor tactics.

## Key Campaigns
The speaker highlights a campaign targeting Hong Kong activists through forum-based water holes in January. A full iOS/iPhone exploit and malware implant chain was discovered and analyzed, revealing the implants were under active development with modifications made over several months.

## Russian Threat Actor Evolution
The speaker references a 2018 security analyst summit presentation on Russian threat actors (referred to as "bears") and their strategic shift eastward. A key prediction—that traditional flagship implants like x-agent (also called splm) would decline—has materialized. By early 2020, new .NET variants of x-tunnel were observed in Central European telecom targets, indicating a broader shift toward zebra-c tooling rather than traditional malware families. Traditional tools like splm downloaders have "completely fallen off the map," replaced by newer, lower-volume downloaders and server-side approaches.

## Server-Side Scanning Tactics
Throughout 2019, multiple reports documented Russian threat actors scanning Exchange servers for vulnerabilities. Interest also extended to SQL servers and SMB servers exposed on the internet, representing a significant tactical shift from traditional malware deployment toward reconnaissance and precise server-side targeting.

## Attribution Challenges
The speaker discusses uncertainty around attribution of activity to "cozy duke," noting a lack of direct evidence linking wellness-related findings to this group. Despite statements attributing this activity to cozy duke, the speaker indicates ongoing investigation and plans for colleagues to present more detailed findings at a future webinar. Activity has been tracked since 2018.

## Takeaways
Russian threat actor behavior continues evolving toward targeted server-side scanning, precision targeting in Asia and Central Asia, and away from traditional implant deployment. Attribution remains complex, with public statements sometimes outpacing investigative confidence.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Is Advanced Endpoint Security a commodity for Business?.
talks.summary:
### Overview
The presentation explores modern endpoint cybersecurity challenges, questioning the traditional two-pronged strategy where basic tools handle mass threats while separate advanced solutions tackle complex, targeted attacks. In large-scale enterprise environments safeguarding tens of thousands of endpoints, even a 0.1% breach rate is critical. As cyber attacks continually evolve, traditional tools fall short, necessitating integrated platforms that span all levels of protection to counter targeted and advanced threats.

### Key Topics
- Limitations of two-pronged and traditional security approaches when managing thousands of endpoints.
- The criticality of small threat margins (e.g., 0.1% unhandled threats) in modern digital environments.
- Unifying threat categories and protection layers through advanced endpoint security platforms.
- Machine learning and artificial intelligence integration for real-time, global threat neutralization.

### Technical Details
The presentation highlights Kaspersky Endpoint Security, framed as a new-generation platform designed to counter current and future threats:
- **Architecture and Deployment**: Operates across physical, virtual, and mobile endpoints (including workstations and critical servers) without demanding changes to existing corporate infrastructure or processes.
- **Core Capabilities**: Detects and halts malicious object delivery, governs application execution, and rolls back systems to their pre-infected states.
- **Behavioral & Correlation Analysis**: Analyzes objects at all protection stages on an additional meta-layer, exposing complex correlations among events and behavioral patterns to construct full threat context.
- **Machine Learning & AI Cloud Integration**: Leverages machine learning algorithms alongside a unified, AI-driven global threat database. Threat intelligence updates instantaneously and automatically across all connected enterprises whenever a new threat attempts an attack anywhere on the network.
- **Reliability**: Engineered to neutralize threats without generating false positives, with validation cited from industry analysts, independent test laboratories, and customers.

### Takeaways
- Relying on separate basic tools for mass threats and advanced tools for targeted attacks leaves vulnerabilities that become significant at scale.
- Effective modern defense requires breaking down boundaries between threat categories with an integrated endpoint platform.
- Automated, cloud-synchronized threat intelligence sharing ensures that defense against an attack on one enterprise immediately shields all other network participants.

talks.summary:
Overview
This talk addresses the financial and operational challenges of manual incident management and presents Kaspersky Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) as a solution to automate incident response while maintaining protection against advanced threats.

Key Challenge
The speaker cites a striking statistic: 52% of companies struggle to distinguish significant security incidents from those that can lead to advanced persistent threats (APTs). Manual gathering, analysis, and validation of incidents is expensive, time-consuming, and requires specialized expertise. Cyberattacks cost businesses between $456,000 and $1.2 million on average, with costs doubling if detection and mitigation fail. This has made cybersecurity a top management priority amid widespread digital transformation.

Incident Management Workflow
The speaker outlines the ideal incident management process in five stages:
1. Data Collection—gathering user and application activity data across the network
2. Visualization & Monitoring—presenting raw data in meaningful context for security specialists
3. Incident Detection—using either threat hunting (manual/semi-automated, leveraging indicators of compromise and expert judgment) or automated detection (combining sandboxing and machine learning)
4. Validation—distinguishing harmless issues from genuine threats
5. Response—taking action to prevent or mitigate identified threats

The Manual Process Problem
When executed manually, this workflow overwhelms IT teams. Many organizations get stuck at steps 1–3 and lack resources to proceed to validation and response, leaving threats unaddressed.

Kaspersky EDR Solution
Kaspersky Endpoint Detection and Response automates the first two workflow steps, freeing IT specialists to focus on critical validation and response work. The solution combines five core elements: monitoring, aggregation, detection, response, and prevention. Built on 20 years of expertise, it operates as an on-premises solution for privacy compliance, integrates with existing endpoint protection (including third-party solutions), and requires no additional software if Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Business is already deployed.

Key Takeaways
Endpoint Detection and Response reduces costs without compromising protection by automating security processes, lowering advanced threat risk, eliminating the need for additional IT staff, and optimizing the capabilities of existing security teams. The solution helps prevent business disruption from advanced threats.

talks.title: Cyber Pulse: The State of Cybersecurity in Healthcare
talks.teaser: Part 2 explores Cyber Pulse: The State of Cybersecurity in Healthcare.
talks.summary:
### Overview
With information-sharing systems proliferating across healthcare environments, safeguarding sensitive patient data has become critical. As of January 2019, over 200 US healthcare organizations suffered IT or hacking-related incidents that affected 500 or more patients. Breached healthcare providers face significant recovery costs, spending an average of $408 per patient to recover healthcare records and up to $1.7 million in advertising to address reputational damage. To explore the factors driving these issues, Kaspersky commissioned a survey of nearly 2,000 healthcare employees across the United States and Canada, evaluating regulatory awareness, security policies, training, and device security protection.

### Key Topics
- **Regulatory Awareness:** Longstanding frameworks exist—such as HIPAA instituted in 1996 in the US and PIPEDA/PIPA in 2000 in Canada—yet organizations struggle to make staff aware of compliance mandates.
- **Security Policies & Governance:** The necessity of establishing and communicating clear cybersecurity policies so staff understand their role in incident prevention and mitigation.
- **Cybersecurity Training:** Developing a culture of vigilance where personnel receive initial and recurrent training on identifying threats and handling security incidents.
- **Device Protection & IT Awareness:** Visibility into how IT systems and endpoint devices storing protected health information (PHI) are secured.

### Technical Details
- **Regulatory Gaps:** 18% of surveyed US healthcare workers did not know the meaning of the HIPAA Security Rule. In Canada, where British Columbia and Nova Scotia prohibit storing protected health information in the US, 49% of Canadian healthcare respondents did not know where PHI had to reside.
- **Policy Deficits:** 21% of respondents were unaware of any cybersecurity policy within their organization while acknowledging one should exist. Among organizations with policies, only 17% of employees in medium and enterprise organizations and 10% in smaller organizations reported reading it more than once.
- **Training Shortfalls:** Approximately one-third of US healthcare employees reported never receiving cybersecurity training despite acknowledging they should have, and roughly one-fifth expressed a need for more training. Comparing employee populations, 24% of US respondents and 41% of Canadian respondents had never received cybersecurity training.
- **Device Security Visibility:** 40% of surveyed healthcare staff did not know how their IT devices were protected. Unawareness was inversely correlated with organization size: 53% of employees in small organizations were unaware of device protections, compared to 39% in medium organizations and 36% in large enterprise organizations.

### Takeaways
Healthcare organizations must improve education regarding regulatory requirements, general security awareness, and incident response protocols so workers know how to respond to suspected issues. Furthermore, healthcare providers must not only implement technical controls on systems storing patient data, but actively communicate these protections to staff to ensure organizational adherence and cultivate employee confidence in data protection practices.

talks.summary:
### Overview
This talk features artist D*Face (Dean Stockton), who reflects on his identity as a hybrid artist whose work spans illustration, graphic design, graffiti, and contemporary art. He discusses his creative process, his view of digital technology as an artistic tool, his background with motorcycle culture, and his collaboration with cybersecurity company Kaspersky Lab to inspire the public and encourage social change.

### Key Topics
- **Artistic Identity and Idea Generation:** Stockton describes art as being defined by the person creating it. His own work sits at the intersection of illustration, graphic design, graffiti, and contemporary art. Ideas typically originate as fleeting thoughts, words, or sentences captured on his phone or a bedside notebook upon waking up or drifting off to sleep.
- **Subculture and Community:** He references "rubbers Alliance" (Rebels Alliance), describing it as a motorcycle community focused on lifestyle, culture, and customization.
- **Digital Tools and Traditional Mediums:** Stockton emphasizes that working digitally is a fundamental element of his workflow. He treats computers not as a replacement for traditional methods, but as another essential tool—akin to a "magic pencil" or a pen in a sketchbook—among a plethora of equipment he relies on.
- **Studio vs. Street Art:** Reflecting on two decades of leaving his mark worldwide through murals and stickers, Stockton highlights the differences between studio creation on a computer screen and painting on a street wall. Each medium offers distinct aesthetic qualities and graces that cannot be replicated by the other.
- **The Mural Concept:** The concept behind his mural explores the fast pace of life, memory, and recollection, combining recognizable individual features into a fresh, cohesive composition.
- **Speed, Safety, and Collaboration:** The speaker highlights the relationship between speed and safety, noting that speed requires preparation and avoiding unnecessary risks. He notes his partnership with Kaspersky Lab, highlighting their shared goal of bringing art to the public to make a positive statement and inspire social change.

### Technical Details
Note: The transcript contains minimal cybersecurity technical depth or vulnerability disclosures, as the talk focuses primarily on visual design, artistic techniques, and creative collaboration.
- **Workflow & Tooling:** Stockton relies on computers alongside traditional pens and sketchbooks to draft visuals before transferring them onto physical walls.
- **Safety Concept:** The talk parallels the necessity of safety and preparation when moving fast, contrasting reckless risk-taking with disciplined preparedness.

### Takeaways
- Technology functions as an augmenting tool in creative production rather than replacing physical craft.
- Speed in execution requires intentional preparation and risk mitigation rather than careless haste.
- Cross-disciplinary partnerships, such as the artist's collaboration with Kaspersky Lab, can serve as a medium to reach the public, provoke thought, and inspire social change.

talks.title: Can software keep your pets safe?
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Can software keep your pets safe?.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Oleg Zaytsev, an expert at Kaspersky Lab, shares how he designed and automated his Smart Home with pet safety and comfort as core design requirements. Addressing hazards faced by various domestic animals—including unleashed dogs, cats, turtles, and aquarium fish—the presentation demonstrates how consumer IoT, surveillance scripting, and automated fail-safes can mitigate domestic risks.

### Key Topics
- **Automated Protection for Roaming Pets:** Addressing risks for unleashed dogs such as escaping through open entrance gates, getting crushed by garage doors, or getting struck by reversing vehicles.
- **Event-Driven Video Surveillance:** Deploying video cameras capable of running event scripts (e.g., motion detection) to detect animals—such as a Yorkshire Terrier or intruder animals like a neighbor's cat—and feeding telemetry into the central control system.
- **Aquarium and Terrarium Environment Controls:** Managing water conditions, heating, filtration, lighting, and leak detection for fish and turtles, supported by independent fail-safes.
- **Home Climate vs. Fall Hazards:** Eliminating the danger of cats falling from heights by relying on forced air ventilation instead of opening windows.

### Technical Details
- **Access Restriction Mechanism:** A dedicated smartphone-activated mode ('Dog on premises' in the 'Unleashed dog' section) places automated locks on motorized barriers. When an attempt is made to open or close the garage door while this restriction is active, the Smart Home blocks the command and outputs an audible voice alert.
- **Surveillance Scripting:** Standard surveillance cameras are configured to execute scripts upon motion detection, passing pet movements and intruder alerts directly to the Smart Home control center.
- **Fail-Safe Aquarium Safeguards:** The aquarium system monitors water pumps, filters, and temperature. Secondary protection systems operate independently to prevent abnormal conditions, such as overheating, even if the primary Smart Home automation malfunctions. (Automated feeders are intentionally omitted to preserve human-pet interaction).
- **Turtle Tank Leak Response:** When a leak sensor activates, the Smart Home issues voice announcements throughout the house, sends SMS and email notifications, automatically disables water heaters and filters, and logs the incident on the management screen until manually reset via an 'All clear' button.

### Takeaways
Designing smart home automation requires striking a deliberate balance between convenience, comfort, and security. By integrating responsive sensor scripts, hardware interlocks, multi-channel alerting, and independent fail-safes, automation software can effectively protect pets from household accidents.

talks.title: MASHA AND THESE BEARS
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding MASHA AND THESE BEARS.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Kurt, a principal security researcher on Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT), analyzes significant shifts in the operations of the threat group APT28 (also referred to as Sofacy) heading into 2018. While historically known for Western-focused operations such as targeting NATO, Ukraine, European elections, and the DNC hack, Sofacy has evolved into a more agile and measured actor. Kurt highlights key evolutions in their toolset, infrastructure, development culture, and geographic targeting, specifically their movement further east into Asia.

### Key Topics
- **Targeting Pivot to the Far East**: Moving beyond historical Western targets and Central Asian "-stans", Sofacy expanded operations across Mongolia, Japan, and China in 2018.
- **Target Overlap with Gray Lambert**: A notable compromise occurred on an aerospace and defense conglomerate server in China previously infected with Gray Lambert (a user-mode passive sniffer implant associated with the Lambert actor family).
- **Decline of SPLM / X-Agent**: The traditional heavy C++ backdoor known as SPLM or CHOPSTICK is largely disappearing from active deployments, replaced by smaller in-memory modules and new frameworks.
- **Rise of Zebrocy**: A subgroup of Sofacy utilizing modular .NET and PowerShell tools, distinct IP-based infrastructure, and rapidly iterating codebases.

### Technical Details
- **Malware Evolution**: Historically, Sofacy maintained consistent C++ codebases over long periods (2004–2009 and 2009–2015). By 2017–2018, the ~300 KB fully featured SPLM backdoor—which bundled keyloggers, remote shells, and file-stealing capabilities communicating over HTTP, FTP, or SMTP—fell out of widespread use. In 2018, SPLM appeared almost exclusively as small in-memory remote shell modules.
- **Chinese Server Overlap**: Sofacy deployed in-memory components onto a Chinese aerospace server shortly after Kaspersky cleaned up Gray Lambert. Hypothesized infection vectors include shared vulnerable web application exploitation (most likely), replay of recorded Lambert magic-value sessions, Lambert false flags, or stolen Sofacy tooling.
- **Cryptography Comparison**: Sofacy's 2017 in-memory plugins use a custom 32-round feedback-based cipher recompiled per victim with changing operators and constraints (distinct from NSA's Speck algorithm). In 2016 (DNC hack), they used simpler sequential XOR operations. In contrast, threat group Turla demonstrates professional standard cryptography (RSA, DES, 3DES) coupled with immature commentary, while Zebrocy implements simpler, practical custom crypto routines.
- **Zebrocy Characteristics**: Zebrocy relies on .NET and PowerShell rather than C++, incorporating USB/removable drive monitoring to exfiltrate files and borrowing open-source tooling such as PowerShell Empire. Zebrocy also utilizes configuration INI files with build ID formatting reminiscent of BlackEnergy's 2014 custom plugins.
- **Infrastructure Shifts**: Traditional Sofacy infrastructure relied on domain names registered via privacy services and paid using Bitcoin. Zebrocy and newer operations have moved toward bare IP addresses, eliminating the need for domain anonymity services.

### Takeaways
Into 2018 and beyond, Sofacy operations demonstrate heightened agility. Defenders must anticipate continuing abandonment of legacy C++ code in favor of modular .NET, PowerShell, and open-source frameworks, continued diversification away from domain-centric infrastructure toward IP-based command-and-control, and broadened geographic targeting across East Asia.

talks.title: What is Spyware?
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding What is Spyware?.
talks.summary:
## Overview
This educational video explains what spyware is and its threat landscape. Spyware is defined as software designed to gather data from a device and communicate personal and confidential information to malicious actors. The presentation emphasizes that any device connected to the Internet is at risk of spyware infestation.

## Infection Methods
The transcript identifies four primary ways spyware infects devices:
1. **Trojans and Social Engineering**: Spyware disguised as legitimate software, using social engineering tactics to trick users into executing malicious code.
2. **Bundled with Legitimate Programs**: Exploitation of user interactions with adware, freeware, and riskyware, as well as interactions with advertisements and adult content.
3. **Tracking Cookies**: Compromised tracking cookies commonly employed by websites.
4. **System Monitors**: Tools designed to monitor computer activity and performance that can be exploited.

## Consequences of Infection
Once installed, spyware causes significant damage:
- **Data Theft**: Compromises email activity, passwords, social media accounts, credit card information, and purchase history; threatens online identity and enables imitation fraud.
- **Performance Degradation**: Consumes device resources, causing slowness, application crashes, and overheating.
- **Malicious Redirection**: Manipulates search results and displays fraudulent websites that trick users into further infections.

## Prevention and Mitigation
The video recommends a layered defense approach:
- **Safe Browsing Practices**: Avoid clicking unexpected email links and suspicious websites.
- **Security Solutions**: Use trusted internet security software for early detection and proactive protection.
- **Removal Tools**: Deploy spyware removal tools for already-infected devices to identify and eliminate threats.

## Takeaways
Spyware poses multifaceted threats combining data theft, privacy violation, and system compromise. Prevention through vigilant browsing and professional security tools remains the most practical defense strategy.

Overview
This transcript does not appear to be from a cybersecurity conference. Instead, it is a talk by Ben, an international street artist, about his artistic practice, creative journey, and philosophy.

Content Summary
Ben describes his transition from graffiti to street art, driven by a lifelong interest in typography and letter forms. He mentions painting in the White House and having lunch with a Prime Minister, though details are sparse. He has spent much of his adult life in East London, which he describes as vibrant, exciting, and cosmopolitan, with extensive coverage of his work throughout the area.

Artistic Philosophy
Ben emphasizes the importance of security in his creative process—both for protecting his ideas while developing them in his studio and for safeguarding his work as it enters the world. He expresses a general sentiment that security matters to everyone: "everybody wants their houses to be secure their banks to be secure" and notes that data security is increasingly important.

A collaboration is mentioned between Ben (as a street artist) and an unnamed "security giant" company described as an engineer. He credits this company as one of the better organizations sponsoring and supporting the arts and creative industries.

Artistic Process
Ben takes pride in creating work from the ground up—stretching canvases, printing, drawing, cutting stencils, and spray-painting himself. He emphasizes the importance of direct personal involvement in all aspects of creation. He expresses a strong preference for colorful artwork and collects art himself. He particularly values one-of-a-kind pieces because of the time, effort, passion, and dedication invested in them, though he admits sadness at parting with finished work once signed.

Takeaways

talks.summary:
### Overview
Cyber-bullying is identified as a rapidly growing worldwide issue that directly affects children and their mental well-being. This presentation outlines the top ten common forms of cyber-bullying to equip parents with the necessary knowledge to identify these behaviors and protect their children.

### Key Topics & Forms of Cyber-Bullying
The presentation details ten specific manifestations of cyber-bullying:

1. **Exclusion**: Occurs when a child is deliberately left out of online activities, conversations, or social media tags. Children lacking the latest technology, such as mobile phones, are noted to be particularly prone to this form.
2. **Harassment**: Involves sustained, intentional bullying consisting of abusive or threatening messages directed at an individual child or a group, significantly impacting their mental health.
3. **Outing**: The act of publicly humiliating a child or group by sharing private or embarrassing information online without consent. This can also include actions such as reading a child's mobile phone messages out loud.
4. **Cyber Stalking**: A dangerous form of harassment executed through communications like email or social media. It also encompasses situations where adults use the internet to establish contact and arrange meetings with young individuals for abusive purposes.
5. **Fraping**: Happens when an unauthorized party accesses a child's social media account to impersonate them and post inappropriate content under their name. The transcript highlights that rude or inappropriate content posted online may never be fully eradicated, even after deletion.
6. **Fake Profiles**: Involves bullies creating deceptive accounts to mask their real identity while harassing a child, or utilizing someone else's email or mobile phone to send harassing messages.
7. **Dissing**: Spreading or posting cruel information, damaging photographs, screenshots, or videos online to tarnish a child's reputation or damage their relationships and friendships.
8. **Trickery**: The act of befriending a child to gain their trust and lure them into a false sense of security, solely to acquire secrets and subsequently share that private information publicly with others.
9. **Trolling**: Deliberately insulting and personally attacking a child on online forums or social media sites to provoke an angry response.
10. **Catfishing**: Stealing online identities to recreate social media profiles for deceptive purposes. Catfishers harvest information from a child's profile to build a fake persona, potentially jeopardizing the child's online reputation.

### Technical Details
While the talk does not cover deep-dive technical vulnerabilities or exploit code, it focuses on platforms and methods used by perpetrators, including compromised credentials/unauthorized access (fraping), identity spoofing and creation of fraudulent accounts (fake profiles, catfishing), communication channels (email, mobile messaging, social networks, forums), and digital persistence risks (content remaining online permanently despite deletion).

### Takeaways
- Parents must stay vigilant regarding the diverse digital tactics bullies use, ranging from passive exclusion to active harassment and social engineering (trickery).
- Online actions carry lasting consequences, as posted material can remain accessible indefinitely.
- Raising awareness among parents and sharing educational resources is essential to recognizing abuse early and putting an end to cyber-bullying.

talks.title: The need for security in transportation
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning The need for security in transportation.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Kurt Baumgartner, a principal security researcher with Kaspersky Lab's Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT), discusses the growing cybersecurity risks within the transportation sector driven by the Internet of Things (IoT). Baumgartner explains that the rapid adoption of connected technologies across global logistics hubs, ports, and passenger vehicles is dramatically increasing attack surfaces while creating critical dependencies on potentially insecure systems.

### Key Topics
- **Maritime and Port Logistics:** Baumgartner highlights ports such as a facility in Latvia that handles 250,000 tons of hazardous chemical substances annually with a staff of only 10 people operating around the clock. He points out that this setup requires heavy reliance on management consoles, Wi-Fi, and online systems. Larger ports in Europe move around 200 million tons of cargo per year, while even larger facilities in India and Singapore similarly depend on small teams and interconnected digital infrastructure.
- **Automotive Surface and Connectivity:** With 250 million cars in the United States and growing vehicle counts in China, modern vehicles have become complex processing hubs. Modern cars feature around 60 different computer systems or CAN buses. The integration of cellular connections, Wi-Fi, telematics, satellite links, keyless entry, tire pressure monitoring, and ignition control exposes hundreds of millions of lines of code that were often developed without security as a primary design goal.
- **Public Hub and Consumer IoT Insecurities:** The speaker addresses vulnerabilities found across private consumer devices (refrigerators, coffee makers, TVs, baby monitors) and public infrastructure like CCTV and surveillance networks used in airports and shipping ports. Public implementations often suffer from plain text transmissions, disabled or missing WPA2, default administrative credentials, and unauthenticated debug ports.

### Technical Details
- **Automotive Exploits Timeline:** Baumgartner cites 2010 research from the University of Washington and University of California, San Diego, where researchers injected messages into a vehicle's CAN bus to achieve complete local control. He contrasts this with the 2015 research by Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek, who demonstrated remote car hacking that led to the recall of 1.4 million vehicles. This attack exploited the Sprint cellular network, which allowed cross-device communication between endpoints, permitting unauthorized access to exposed vehicle ports.
- **Satellite Abuse by Threat Actors:** Kaspersky's research identified APT groups actively exploiting unencrypted or vulnerable legacy satellite communications. Specifically, Baumgartner references the Turla APT and Poseidon APT groups abusing legacy satellite links that cannot be easily updated or patched.

### Takeaways
Baumgartner emphasizes that the transportation industry faces systemic cyber risks, noting that surveys of transportation organizations show nearly all have experienced internal or external security incidents. Vendor responses claiming that security issues will be addressed in the next hardware model fail to solve existing risks, particularly for legacy and critical infrastructure. Baumgartner calls for earlier security audits, penetration testing, and broader cross-industry collaboration before vulnerable systems are deployed.

talks.title: Security lessons from the Sochi Olympics
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Security lessons from the Sochi Olympics.
talks.summary:
Overview
This talk covers security operations and incident response during the Sochi Olympic Games. The security team managed up to 70 incidents daily while retrofitting security measures into infrastructure that was not originally designed with security in mind. Despite the high incident volume, no breaches were publicly announced.

Key Challenge: The Journalist Factor
The speaker emphasizes that 13,000 journalists attending the games created an unexpected security variable. These journalists had built automated monitoring systems for the Olympic infrastructure and could publish articles about security issues within minutes of their occurrence. A DDoS attack lasting only three minutes resulted in article publication within two minutes of the attack start.

Four Major Incidents

1. FTP Server Breach (New Year's Eve): Stolen FTP accounts were being sold for $10,000 per account on hacking forums. The compromised server had improper configuration and direct access to the domain controller. Analysis revealed Wireshark installation, deleted logs, and 50+ compromised accounts including administrative and security officer accounts.

2. Undetected Brazilian Bank Trojan: Using AVZ malware detection technology (which automatically processes logs and quarantines), the team discovered specially crafted malware initially undetected by any antivirus. The same malware appeared in modified form two months later and again one month after that. Analysis revealed it targeted the finance department, stealing banking client accounts, AD credentials, and VPN accounts.

3. Botnet Discovery: During forensics work for another customer, the team found references to Olympic infrastructure IP addresses in botnet configuration files. This led to discovery of three additional botnets, with detailed analysis showing significant data theft and account compromises.

4. Insider Threat (4 AM Incident): A first-line network engineer was discovered conducting suspicious activities including disk wiping tools, cryptography tools, malware tools (Metasploit), and antivirus evasion attempts. Investigation revealed he was a previously convicted attacker (multiple federal website attacks) who had gained employment using false identity and was preparing a serious attack on critical Olympic resources.

Defensive Measures and Results
The team deployed multiple APT detection services, cyber intelligence platforms, and AVZ-based automated malware analysis. Overall statistics: 100,000+ malware attacks prevented (primarily trojans and Java exploits) and 2,000+ attacks detected on honeypot systems.

Lessons Learned
- Secure by design: integrate security from inception, not retrofit
- Invest in quality people and best-in-class tools (Kaspersky Lab technology)
- Customer education and building client confidence in expertise is essential

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Tor and the Average Internet User, Runa Sandvick, Tor Project advocate.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk excerpt, the speaker discusses the practical importance of Tor for everyday internet users, beyond just specialized groups like journalists and human rights activists. The presentation highlights how Tor allows individuals to regain control of their online privacy by concealing web browsing activities from local observers and websites alike, while also serving as a tool for censorship circumvention.

### Key Topics
- **Online Privacy for Normal Users**: How everyday users can use Tor to ensure their internet service provider (ISP), employers, or shared computer users cannot monitor which websites they visit, and prevent websites from knowing who is visiting them.
- **The "Anonymity Loves Company" Principle**: Tor relies on a broad and diverse user base. When average users adopt Tor, it directly strengthens anonymity and security for high-risk users, such as human rights activists and journalists who depend on the network.
- **Censorship Circumvention**: Tor provides the ability to bypass network restrictions or national censorship when specific websites are blocked.
- **Data Profiling and Tracking**: Commercial entities collect and analyze online activities to build behavioral profiles, often deducing personal information without explicit disclosure.

### Technical Details
*(Note: The provided transcript excerpt contains limited technical detail regarding the underlying Tor architecture or protocol implementations.)*
- Tor obscures traffic bidirectionally: ISPs and local network observers cannot see the destination websites, and destination websites cannot identify the originating visitor.
- Data aggregation is contrasted against Tor's privacy guarantees: corporate tracking analyzes patterns in online behavior and shopping habits to deduce sensitive private details, illustrated by an example of Target identifying a teenage customer's pregnancy through shifts in product purchasing habits.

### Takeaways
- Tor is not only for high-profile or high-risk individuals; everyday users benefit directly by shielding their online habits from recording, analysis, and profiling.
- Widespread adoption of Tor by ordinary internet users is vital to the entire anonymity ecosystem, providing safety in numbers for everyone using the system.
- Tor serves both privacy protection and access enablement by bypassing local network and geographic website blocks.

### Overview
This guide outlines the components, prerequisites, and step-by-step installation process for Kaspersky Small Office Security 3. The package bundles Kaspersky Small Office Security for Personal Computer, Kaspersky Small Office Security for File Server, and Kaspersky Internet Security for Android for mobile devices.

### Key Topics
- **Package Components:** Covers the distribution containing software for personal computers, file servers, and Android mobile devices.
- **Pre-Installation Requirements:** Checklist of preparatory steps before launching the setup wizard, such as verifying system requirements and checking for incompatible software.
- **Installation Media & Methods:** Starting setup via physical CD media or through a downloaded setup executable purchased from an online store.

# Overview
Working with online banking or payment systems requires specialized protection, as the loss of confidential data can result in financial losses. The Safe Money service included in Kaspersky Internet Security 2014 provides a secure environment to safeguard banking and payment operations.

# Key Topics
- **Default Behavior and Automatic Prompts**: The Safe Money component is enabled by default. When an online banking system or personal cabinet of a payment system is accessed, the application prompts the user to open the web page inside a protected browser. Users can select the option to remember this choice so the website automatically opens in a protected browser during future visits.
- **Manual Website Configuration**: Users can manually register specific online banking and payment websites directly within the Safe Money interface.
- **Browser Selection**: Although Safe Money opens sites using the operating system's default browser by default, users can customize which browser is used for secure sessions.

# Technical Details
- **Component Prerequisites**: Safe Money requires the application's self-defense feature to be enabled; otherwise, the component does not function.
- **Required Browser Plugins**: For proper operation and loading of protected web pages, four browser plugins must be installed:
  - Content Blocker
  - Safe Money
  - Virtual Keyboard
  - URL Advisor
- **Verifying Protection Status**: To verify that protection is active, navigate to the application settings window, select "Protection Center", and verify that the Safe Money component is enabled in the right pane.
- **Adding Websites Manually**: From the main application window, select "Safe Money", click "Add bank or payment system", input the website address and description, and select the desired action (such as "Run protected browser"). After saving, the link is listed in the Safe Money window for direct launch.
- **Configuring Browser Choice**: To choose a specific browser rather than the OS default, open the settings window, go to "Protection Center", select "Safe Money" in the right pane, and pick the desired browser from the dropdown list located in the "Additional" section.
- **Troubleshooting**: If a protected webpage fails to load, ensure all required plugins (Content Blocker, Safe Money, Virtual Keyboard, URL Advisor) are installed and active in the protected browser.

# Takeaways
Kaspersky Internet Security 2014 secures financial operations through its Safe Money component and protected browser technology. Reliable protection depends on enabling application self-defense, configuring target financial URLs, and maintaining all required security plugins across the selected web browser.
